modules.title: Program Design
modules.summary: Welcome to the Technical Program Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: Program Design. Program design is the TPM's core artifact: turning an ambiguous mandate into scope, milestones, dependencies, risks, and a communication plan that survives contact with four teams and two time zones. By the end of this module you will be able to scope an ambiguous initiative on the fly, map milestones and dependencies explicitly, define success criteria with real exit conditions, and walk an interviewer through a program brief the way the case rounds score it.
objectives: Understand and apply: scoping ambiguous initiatives
Understand and apply: milestones and dependency mapping
Understand and apply: defining success criteria and exit conditions
Understand and apply: risk registers and mitigation plans
Understand and apply: stakeholder mapping

notes.title: Concepts

notes.body: Preparation only — this module confers no certificate and grants no credential. TPM case rounds score how you structure ambiguity, and the strongest answers are built from your own real programs: use the frameworks here to organize your own experience, not to narrate someone else's. Interviewers can always tell the difference.

notes.title: Worked example: Program Design
notes.body:
**Problem.** The TPM's core artifact for ambiguity is:
A. A timeline
B. Scope, milestones, dependencies, risks, and a comms plan ←
C. A staffing plan
D. A budget spreadsheet

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Program Design — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: A (A timeline); C (A staffing plan); D (A budget spreadsheet) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: B. Program design turns an ambiguous mandate into executable structure — the Concepts note lists every piece of the artifact.

**Solution.** B — Scope, milestones, dependencies, risks, and a comms plan

notes.title: Common mistakes: Program Design

cards.front: What turns an ambiguous mandate into a program?
cards.back: Scope, milestones, dependency map, success criteria with exit conditions, risk register, stakeholder map, and a communication cadence — the TPM’s core artifact.
Hidden dependencies are where programs die — the map makes them visible, owned, and sequenced before they become surprises.

cards.front: What are success criteria with exit conditions?
cards.back: The measurable definition of done plus the conditions under which you stop — preventing zombie programs that never end.

cards.front: What goes in a risk register?
cards.back: Each risk, its likelihood and impact, mitigations, and an owner — reviewed on a cadence, not filed away.
Right information to right stakeholders at the right rhythm — preventing both surprise escalations and meeting sprawl.
A checklist proving the program can ship: owners, rollback, comms, and support — readiness verified, not assumed.

cards.front: What is the TPM's core artifact for ambiguity?
cards.back: Scope, milestones, dependency maps, risk register, stakeholder map, and comms cadence — the program design.

The TPM's core artifact: turning an ambiguous mandate into scope, milestones, dependency maps, risks, and a communication plan.

handsOnLab.brief: You will build a complete interview story bank for this module's topics and rehearse it under timed conditions: six stories in situation→decision→outcome→lesson format, two disagreement stories, and your questions for the panel. steps: List the six stories this module demands (Understand and apply: system design literacy for non-coders). For each, draft the 4-part structure: situation (2 sentences), your decision, the outcome with a number, the lesson.

Cut every story to a 3-minute spoken version. Time yourself reading aloud — cut filler until each lands under the limit.
Record yourself answering three stories on your phone. Listen back and score: structure (0-2), specificity (0-2), conciseness (0-2).

modules.summary: Welcome to the Engineering Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: People Leadership. The people half of the EM role: 1:1s, feedback, coaching, and the hard conversations — taught as skills with reps, not traits you either have or do not. By the end of this module you will run 1:1s that belong to the report, give feedback that lands, choose coaching over managing when the moment needs it, handle performance management fairly, and build psychological safety by how you react to bad news, daily.

modules.title: Product Sense
modules.summary: Welcome to the Product Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: Product Sense. Product sense is structured empathy: clarifying the user and the problem before any solution, prioritizing with stated assumptions, and critiquing products by mechanism rather than taste. By the end of this module you will show user empathy with specific humans, frame problems before solutions, ask 'why' honestly five times, read markets and competitors, prioritize with impact versus effort and stated assumptions, and structure open-ended product questions so the interviewer can follow your thinking.
objectives: Understand and apply: user empathy: who, and what hurts
Understand and apply: problem framing before solutions
Understand and apply: asking ‘why’ five times, honestly
Understand and apply: market and competitive understanding
Understand and apply: prioritization: impact versus effort, with assumptions stated

notes.body: Preparation only — this module confers no certificate and grants no credential. Product sense cannot be faked from frameworks alone: critique products you actually use, empathize with users you actually understand, and never present a market read you have not actually done. modules.summary: Welcome back to the PM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Metrics and Judgment. Metrics separate PMs who guess from PMs who learn: defining measures that track user value, reading experiments honestly, and debugging moves before reacting to them. By the end of this module you will define success metrics tied to user value, read funnels and cohorts fluently, design A/B tests with significance discipline, debug a moved metric before reacting, estimate sanely, make judgment calls with incomplete data, and spot the failure modes of north-star metrics.
objectives: Understand and apply: defining success metrics tied to user value
Understand and apply: analytics literacy: funnels, cohorts, retention
Understand and apply: A/B testing: design, significance, and pitfalls
Understand and apply: debugging a metric that moved
Understand and apply: estimation questions done sanely

3. Confirm the survivor: A. The Concepts glossary defines a good success metric as tied to user value, measurable, with known failure modes — tracking learning, not vanity.

**Solution.** A — Tied to user value, with failure modes known

modules.summary: Welcome to the Technical Product Management track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 1: Technical Depth for PMs. Enough engineering to be dangerous in the good way: how systems are built, where they break, and how to reason about scale — the depth technical PM interviews actually test. By the end of this module you will reason about the web at PM altitude, compare databases by access pattern, weigh caching's speed against staleness, use queues for async scale, read technical docs for commitments, and estimate scale with sane round-number math.

This module covers design tradeoffs, versioning discipline, and the unglamorous contract work that decides whether a platform gets adopted. By the end of this module you will discuss REST tradeoffs credibly, weigh versioning as a compatibility promise, choose between webhooks and polling deliberately, think in platforms versus products, and treat developer experience as the product.

Understand and apply: versioning and compatibility promises

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Data Literacy for PMs
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a complete interview story bank for this module's topics and rehearse it under timed conditions: six stories in situation→decision→outcome→lesson format, two disagreement stories, and your questions for the panel. The deliverable is the written bank plus a self-scored rehearsal log.
steps: List the six stories this module demands (Understand and apply: SQL literacy: joins, aggregations, windows). For each, draft the 4-part structure: situation (2 sentences), your decision, the outcome with a number, the lesson.
Write two disagreement stories: one where data changed your mind, one where you held your ground. Include what you said verbatim.
Cut every story to a 3-minute spoken version. Time yourself reading aloud — cut filler until each lands under the limit.
Record yourself answering three stories on your phone. Listen back and score: structure (0-2), specificity (0-2), conciseness (0-2).
Re-answer the lowest-scoring story until it scores 5+. Write down the exact phrases you will reuse.
Draft five questions for the panel (org structure, decision rights, 90-day success, team health, manager style). Finalize the bank.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A story bank document (6+2 stories in 4-part format, all timed under 3 minutes) plus the rehearsal score log.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every story has a number in the outcome; every story lands under 3 minutes spoken; disagreement stories include verbatim quotes.

modules.title: Technical Design Reps
modules.summary: Welcome back to the Technical PM track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 5: Technical Design Reps. Design reps calibrated for PMs: you will not out-architect the engineers, but you will connect architecture choices to user outcomes, cost, and iteration speed — and record the tradeoffs. By the end of this module you will perform the PM system-design interview format, reason about 10x and 100x scaling, weigh cost versus latency versus complexity, hold the security basics, contribute the PM's lens in architecture reviews, document decisions and tradeoffs, and know the limits of your depth.
objectives: Understand and apply: system design for PMs: the interview format
Understand and apply: scaling reasoning: 10x, 100x
Understand and apply: cost versus latency versus complexity
Understand and apply: security basics for PMs
Understand and apply: participating in architecture reviews

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
Project brief
Honesty note
notes.body: Preparation only — this module confers no certificate and grants no credential. Design reps must be performed on systems you genuinely understand — the format rewards the PM's lens, not borrowed architecture. Never out-architect the engineers in the room; narrate your own reasoning honestly and defer where your depth ends.

notes.title: Worked example: Technical Design Reps
notes.body:
**Problem.** PM design interviews ask you to:
A. Stay silent
B. Draw boxes silently
C. Narrate choices to user outcomes, cost, and iteration speed ←
D. Out-architect engineers

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Technical Design Reps — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: A (Stay silent); B (Draw boxes silently); D (Out-architect engineers) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: C. The Concepts glossary defines the PM system-design format as narrating architecture choices tied to user outcomes — you will not out-architect the engineers, and should not try.

**Solution.** C — Narrate choices to user outcomes, cost, and iteration speed

*Try it yourself:* cover the solution, re-answer from memory, then check. If you missed it, re-read the Concepts note before moving on.

modules.summary: Welcome back to the GenAI track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: LLM Product Patterns. The recurring shapes of LLM products — chat, copilots, agents, RAG — with guidance on matching the pattern to the problem instead of defaulting to a chatbot. By the end of this module you will name the chat pattern's traps, design copilots inside existing workflows, judge when agents fit, apply RAG for grounded knowledge tasks, use summarization and transformation patterns, choose patterns deliberately, and iterate with eval-driven prompt and system design.

modules.title: Risk and Responsibility
modules.summary: Welcome back to the GenAI track — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 5: Risk and Responsibility. The risk half of shipping AI: bias, privacy, safety, and misuse — taught as product decisions with owners and mitigations, not as abstract ethics. By the end of this module you will assess bias and fairness on your use case, manage what the model remembers, threat-model safety and misuse, scope red-teaming, operationalize responsible AI principles, run AI incident response, and document risk decisions.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Logic & Proof for Technical Leadership Interview Prep
modules.summary: Propositional logic, truth tables, quantifiers, and the four proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction) — the reasoning substrate for policies, algorithms, and security arguments. Prerequisite spine for Technical Leadership Interview Prep.
objectives: Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables and identify tautologies.
Apply De Morgan’s laws and logical equivalences to simplify statements.
Negate quantified statements correctly (∀/∃ duality).
Write direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction proofs.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Technical Leadership Interview Prep
Propositions, connectives, and truth tables
Tautologies, contradictions, and De Morgan’s laws
notes.body: A tautology is true in every row (e.g., p∨¬p); a contradiction is false in every row (p∧¬p). Two formulas are logically equivalent if their tables match column-for-column. Worked example (verified): prove De Morgan’s law ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q by table. Row (T,T): LHS ¬T=F; RHS F∨F=F. Row (T,F): LHS ¬F=T; RHS F∨T=T. Row (F,T): LHS T; RHS T∨F=T. Row (F,F): LHS T; RHS T∨T=T. All four rows agree — equivalence verified. The dual law ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q holds by the same check. These laws are the workhorses of simplifying firewall rules, IAM policies, and boolean search: "not (A and B)" becomes "not-A or not-B". Other key equivalences: contrapositive (p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p), and implication-as-disjunction (p→q ≡ ¬p∨q).

notes.title: Predicates and quantifiers
notes.body: A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is fixed. Quantifiers bind x: ∀x P(x) ("for all x") and ∃x P(x) ("there exists x"). Worked example: let domain be integers, P(x) = "x² ≥ 0". Then ∀x P(x) is TRUE (squares are never negative). Now negate ∀x∃y (y > x) — "for every integer there is a larger one". Negation flips each quantifier and the inner predicate: ∃x∀y (y ≤ x) — "some integer is ≥ every integer", which is FALSE over integers (no maximum). The duality rules: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Common error: negating "all users are admins" as "no users are admins" — the correct negation is "some user is not an admin". In access-control requirements, this distinction is the difference between a correct policy and a breach.

notes.title: Direct proof and proof by contrapositive
notes.body: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion through valid steps. Proof by contrapositive proves ¬q→¬p instead of p→q (equivalent by the table). Worked example: prove "if n² is even, then n is even" for integers. Direct attack stalls (square roots of parity are awkward), so use contrapositive: "if n is odd, then n² is odd". Let n = 2k+1. Then n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Contrapositive proved, so the original holds. Numeric check: n=7 (odd) → 49 (odd) ✓; n=6 (even) → 36 (even) ✓. Choose the method by shape: when the conclusion is a negative or "not" statement, contrapositive usually simplifies; when hypothesis and conclusion are both positive constructions, go direct.

notes.title: Proof by contradiction
notes.body: Assume the negation of what you want, derive an impossibility, and conclude the original. Worked example (classic, verified): prove √2 is irrational. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms (gcd(a,b)=1). Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² — a² is even, hence a is even (by the previous note’s result), a = 2k. Then 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k² — b² is even, hence b is even. But a and b both even contradicts lowest terms. The assumption is impossible; √2 is irrational. The pattern: contradiction proofs shine when the claim says something does NOT exist (no rational square root, no largest prime). Euclid’s proof of infinitely many primes uses the same skeleton: assume finitely many, multiply them and add 1, find a new prime factor — contradiction.

cards.back: A statement that is unambiguously true or false — never both, never neither.

cards.back: Base case P(n₀); inductive step: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

cards.back: Contrapositive: n odd ⇒ n=2k+1 ⇒ n²=2(2k²+2k)+1, odd.

handsOnLab.title: Verify logic by brute force with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify De Morgan’s laws and the contrapositive equivalence by exhaustive truth-table enumeration in Python, then prove a small parity claim both by hand and by exhaustive check. The machine settles every row; your hand proof must agree.
steps: Open python3. Define implies = lambda p,q: (not p) or q.
Enumerate all four (p,q) pairs. For each, compute not (p and q) and (not p) or (not q); assert they are equal on every row — De Morgan verified by brute force.
Repeat for the dual law: not (p or q) vs (not p) and (not q). Assert equality on all rows.
Verify contrapositive: for all rows, implies(p,q) == implies(not q, not p). Print any counterexample (there will be none).
Show the converse is NOT equivalent: find the row where implies(p,q) != implies(q,p). Record it.
Prove by hand on paper: "if n² is odd then n is odd" via contrapositive. Then brute-force check n in range(0,50): assert (n*n % 2 == 1) implies (n % 2 == 1).
Write up: which equivalences held on all rows, the converse counterexample row, and your parity proof.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A short write-up with the brute-force verification output, the converse counterexample, and the hand parity proof.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All assertions pass; the converse counterexample row is identified; the hand proof matches the brute-force check.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Statistics & Probability for Technical Leadership Interview Prep
modules.summary: Descriptive statistics, probability rules, Bayes’ theorem, expectation and variance, the binomial and normal distributions, and hypothesis testing — the math behind evaluation metrics, alert triage, and A/B decisions. Prerequisite spine for Technical Leadership Interview Prep.
objectives: Compute mean, median, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset.
Apply the addition and multiplication rules of probability.
Use Bayes’ theorem to update beliefs with evidence.
Compute expectation and variance of discrete random variables.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Technical Leadership Interview Prep
Describing data: center and spread
Probability rules that never change
notes.body: Sample space S, event A: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1. Addition rule: P(A∪b) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) (subtract the double-counted overlap); for mutually exclusive events the last term is 0. Complement: P(not A) = 1−P(A). Multiplication: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(B|A)=P(B). Worked example (verified): a queue has 30% high-priority tickets (H) and 20% are escalations (E); 12% are both. P(H∪E) = 0.30+0.20−0.12 = 0.38. If instead H and E were independent, P(both) would be 0.30×0.20 = 0.06 ≠ 0.12 — so they are NOT independent (escalations skew high-priority). Two independent deploys each fail with p=0.05: P(both fail) = 0.05² = 0.0025; P(at least one fails) = 1−(0.95)² = 1−0.9025 = 0.0975.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
notes.body: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B): probability of A given B occurred. Bayes inverts the conditioning: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+). Worked example — alert triage (verified): 1% of hosts are compromised (P(D)=0.01). The detector catches 99% of compromised hosts (sensitivity P(+|D)=0.99) and false-alarms on 5% of clean hosts (P(+|¬D)=0.05). P(+) = 0.99×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0099+0.0495 = 0.0594. P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0594 ≈ 0.1667 — only ~16.7%! Most alerts are false positives despite a "99% accurate" detector, because the base rate is tiny. This base-rate effect is the single most important probability lesson for SOC triage, medical screening, and fraud detection: accuracy without the base rate is meaningless. Always expand P(+) via total probability before trusting a positive.

notes.title: Expectation and variance of random variables
notes.body: For discrete X with values xᵢ and probabilities pᵢ: E[X] = Σxᵢpᵢ (long-run average); Var(X) = E[X²]−(E[X])²; SD = √Var. Linearity: E[aX+b] = aE[X]+b, and E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when dependent. Worked example — fair die (verified): E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. E[X²] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.1667. Var = 91/6 − 3.5² = 15.1667−12.25 = 2.9167 = 35/12. SD ≈ 1.708. Worked example 2: a Bernoulli trial with success p has E[X]=p and Var=p(1−p) — variance peaks at p=0.5 (maximum uncertainty). In ML, cross-entropy loss is minimized exactly when predicted probabilities match these expectations; in capacity planning, E[load] sizes the average but Var(load) sizes the headroom.

notes.title: The binomial and normal distributions
notes.body: Binomial(n,p): number of successes in n independent trials; P(X=k) = C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k), E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p). Normal(μ,σ²): the bell curve; the 68-95-99.7 rule says P(|X−μ|<σ)≈0.68, <2σ ≈0.95, <3σ ≈0.997. Worked example — binomial (verified): 5 independent alert rules, each fires spuriously with p=0.3. P(exactly 2 fire) = C(5,2)·0.3²·0.7³ = 10×0.09×0.343 = 0.3087 ≈ 30.9%. Worked example — normal: API latency ~ Normal(μ=120ms, σ=15ms). P(latency > 150) = P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.0228 — about 2.3% of requests. The Central Limit Theorem is why the normal appears everywhere: averages of many small independent effects are approximately normal, which justifies z-intervals for A/B test readouts and poll margins.

handsOnLab.title: Verify probability by simulation with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify the Bayes triage calculation, the binomial probability, and the die variance three ways: by hand formula, by exact computation, and by Monte Carlo simulation. All three must agree.
steps: Open python3. Simulate the Bayes scenario: 1M hosts, 1% compromised; detector: 99% sensitivity, 5% false-alarm. Count positives and the fraction compromised among them; confirm ≈0.167.
Compute exactly: (0.99*0.01)/(0.99*0.01+0.05*0.99). Compare with the simulation to 3 decimals.
Binomial check: from math import comb; compute comb(5,2)*0.3**2*0.7**3; then simulate 200k runs of 5 Bernoulli(0.3) trials and compare the fraction with exactly 2 successes.
Die variance: exact = sum(x*x for x in range(1,7))/6 - 3.5**2; simulate 500k die rolls, compute sample variance; compare.
Break it: change prevalence to 50% in the Bayes simulation and watch P(D|+) jump — record both values to feel the base-rate effect.
Write up: the three agreements (formula vs exact vs simulation) and one sentence on why simulation is a legitimate verification tool.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Write-up with the three verified numbers (Bayes ≈0.1667, binomial ≈0.3087, die variance ≈2.9167) from all three methods.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Simulation, exact computation, and hand formula agree to 2+ decimals on all three quantities.

mockTask.q: Your detector is "99% accurate" and just fired on a host. Base rate of compromise is 1 in 1000, false-alarm rate 5%. What do you tell the on-call?
choices: "Likely a false positive (~2%); investigate normally, don’t page the war room"
mockTask.explain: P(D|+) = (0.99×0.001)/(0.99×0.001+0.05×0.999) ≈ 0.0194 — under 2%. Base rate dominates; respond proportionally.

scriptLabs.title: SQL literacy: joins and windows
scriptLabs.brief: Answer product questions with SQL against an in-memory SQLite database: joins, aggregations, and a window function for cohort-style ranking — the hands-on core of data literacy for PMs.
scriptLabs.starter:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, plan TEXT, country TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE events (user_id INTEGER, event TEXT, day TEXT)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
                [(1, 'pro', 'US'), (2, 'free', 'US'), (3, 'pro', 'DE'), (4, 'free', 'DE')])
con.executemany('INSERT INTO events VALUES (?, ?, ?)', [
    (1, 'signup', '2026-09-01'), (1, 'purchase', '2026-09-03'),
    (2, 'signup', '2026-09-01'), (3, 'signup', '2026-09-02'),
    (3, 'purchase', '2026-09-05'), (4, 'signup', '2026-09-02')])

# TODO 1: conversion rate signup->purchase by plan (JOIN + GROUP BY).
# TODO 2: rank users by event count with a window function.
# Print both result sets.
scriptLabs.hint: Join events to users on user_id; conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN event='purchase' ...)) gives conversions per cohort. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) ranks users.
scriptLabs.solution:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, plan TEXT, country TEXT)')
con.execute('CREATE TABLE events (user_id INTEGER, event TEXT, day TEXT)')
con.executemany('INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
                [(1, 'pro', 'US'), (2, 'free', 'US'), (3, 'pro', 'DE'), (4, 'free', 'DE')])
con.executemany('INSERT INTO events VALUES (?, ?, ?)', [
    (1, 'signup', '2026-09-01'), (1, 'purchase', '2026-09-03'),
    (2, 'signup', '2026-09-01'), (3, 'signup', '2026-09-02'),
    (3, 'purchase', '2026-09-05'), (4, 'signup', '2026-09-02')])

print('--- conversion by plan ---')
for row in con.execute('''
    SELECT u.plan,
           COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS signups,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event = 'purchase' THEN u.id END) AS buyers,
           ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event = 'purchase' THEN u.id END)
                 / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id), 1) AS conv_pct
    FROM users u LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = u.id
    GROUP BY u.plan'''):
    print(row)

print('--- users ranked by activity ---')
for row in con.execute('''
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS events,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS activity_rank
    FROM events GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY activity_rank'''):
    print(row)

scriptLabs.title: Funnel analysis with pandas
scriptLabs.brief: Build a signup→activation→purchase funnel from event data, compute step conversion rates, and find which segment drops off hardest — the analytics literacy PM interviews probe.
scriptLabs.starter:
import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame([
    ('u1', 'pro', 'signup'), ('u1', 'pro', 'activate'), ('u1', 'pro', 'purchase'),
    ('u2', 'free', 'signup'), ('u2', 'free', 'activate'),
    ('u3', 'pro', 'signup'),
    ('u4', 'free', 'signup'), ('u4', 'free', 'activate'), ('u4', 'free', 'purchase'),
    ('u5', 'free', 'signup'),
], columns=['user', 'plan', 'event'])
steps = ['signup', 'activate', 'purchase']

# TODO: for each plan, compute users reaching each step and step-to-step conversion.
# Print a funnel table and name the worst drop-off step per plan.
scriptLabs.hint: Pivot users x steps into a boolean matrix (crosstab), then cumsum across steps can't decrease — use cumulative reach per step and divide successive steps.
scriptLabs.solution:
import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame([
    ('u1', 'pro', 'signup'), ('u1', 'pro', 'activate'), ('u1', 'pro', 'purchase'),
    ('u2', 'free', 'signup'), ('u2', 'free', 'activate'),
    ('u3', 'pro', 'signup'),
    ('u4', 'free', 'signup'), ('u4', 'free', 'activate'), ('u4', 'free', 'purchase'),
    ('u5', 'free', 'signup'),
], columns=['user', 'plan', 'event'])
steps = ['signup', 'activate', 'purchase']

reach = (events.assign(hit=1).pivot_table(index=['plan', 'user'], columns='event',
                                           values='hit', fill_value=0))
# a user 'reaches' a step only if they completed all prior steps
for i, s in enumerate(steps):
    prior = steps[:i + 1]
    reach[s + '_reached'] = (reach[prior].sum(axis=1) == len(prior)).astype(int)

funnel = reach.groupby('plan')[[s + '_reached' for s in steps]].sum()
print('--- funnel: users reaching each step ---')
print(funnel)
print('--- step conversion ---')
conv = funnel.copy()
for i in range(1, len(steps)):
    conv[steps[i]] = funnel[steps[i] + '_reached'] / funnel[steps[i - 1] + '_reached']
print(conv[steps[1:]].round(2))
worst = (1 - conv[steps[1:]]).idxmax(axis=1)
print('worst drop-off step per plan:')
print(worst)

scriptLabs.title: A/B test significance, sanely
scriptLabs.brief: Compute conversion rates, lift, and a z-test for a two-variant experiment — the design-significance-pitfalls triad from the metrics module, in code.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math

# Variant A: 120 conversions / 4000 visitors; Variant B: 150 / 4000.
def ab_test(conv_a, n_a, conv_b, n_b):
    # TODO: compute rates, lift, pooled SE, z-score, two-sided p-value (normal approx).
    # Return a dict and print a one-line verdict at alpha=0.05.
    ...

ab_test(120, 4000, 150, 4000)
scriptLabs.hint: Pooled p = (conv_a+conv_b)/(n_a+n_b); SE = sqrt(p(1-p)(1/n_a+1/n_b)); z = (rate_b-rate_a)/SE; two-sided p via math.erf.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math

def ab_test(conv_a, n_a, conv_b, n_b, alpha=0.05):
    ra, rb = conv_a / n_a, conv_b / n_b
    lift = (rb - ra) / ra
    p_pool = (conv_a + conv_b) / (n_a + n_b)
    se = math.sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1 / n_a + 1 / n_b))
    z = (rb - ra) / se
    p = 2 * (1 - 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(abs(z) / math.sqrt(2))))
    verdict = 'significant' if p < alpha else 'not significant'
    print(f'A: {ra:.3%}  B: {rb:.3%}  lift: {lift:+.1%}  z={z:.2f}  p={p:.4f} -> {verdict} at alpha={alpha}')
    return {'rate_a': ra, 'rate_b': rb, 'lift': lift, 'z': z, 'p': p}

ab_test(120, 4000, 150, 4000)
print('Pitfalls to state in the interview: peeking inflates false positives; '
      'significance is not importance (check the absolute lift); '
      'segment before celebrating.')

scriptLabs.title: Back-of-envelope capacity estimation
scriptLabs.brief: Do the scaling math technical-PM interviews expect: from DAU and requests/user/day to RPS, storage, and bandwidth — with explicit assumptions stated.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Scenario: 2M DAU, avg 40 requests/user/day, avg response 20 KB,
# avg write 2 KB stored per request, 30-day retention, peak = 3x average.
# TODO: compute avg RPS, peak RPS, daily storage, 30-day storage,
# and daily egress bandwidth. Print each with the assumption chain.
DAU = 2_000_000
REQ_PER_USER_DAY = 40
scriptLabs.hint: RPS = DAU * req/user/day / 86400. State every assumption; interviewers grade the reasoning chain, not the final number.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Assumptions: 2M DAU, 40 req/user/day, 20 KB avg response,
# 2 KB stored per request, 30-day retention, peak = 3x average.
DAU = 2_000_000
REQ_PER_USER_DAY = 40
AVG_RESP_KB = 20
STORED_KB = 2
RETENTION_DAYS = 30
PEAK_FACTOR = 3

avg_rps = DAU * REQ_PER_USER_DAY / 86400
peak_rps = avg_rps * PEAK_FACTOR
daily_storage_gb = DAU * REQ_PER_USER_DAY * STORED_KB / 1e6
retention_gb = daily_storage_gb * RETENTION_DAYS
daily_egress_tb = DAU * REQ_PER_USER_DAY * AVG_RESP_KB / 1e9

print(f'avg RPS: {avg_rps:,.0f} | peak RPS: {peak_rps:,.0f}')
print(f'daily storage: {daily_storage_gb:,.0f} GB | 30-day: {retention_gb:,.0f} GB')
print(f'daily egress bandwidth: {daily_egress_tb:.1f} TB')  # bandwidth = response bytes served
print('Interview rule: narrate assumptions first, do round-number math, '
      'and sanity-check the answer (does ~1k RPS feel right for 2M DAU?).')

scenarios.title: Leading through an incident
scenarios.context: You are the EM on call. Checkout is down, the war room has 14 people, two teams blame each other’s deploy, and the CEO is asking for an ETA in the channel.

options.text: Assign blame, then debug
options.why: Blame freezes the room — the incident needs mitigation first, attribution later in the postmortem.

options.text: Declare yourself incident commander, split the room into mitigation and comms, set a 15-minute update cadence
options.why: The EM scenario reps teach: take command, parallelize mitigation vs communication, and make status predictable — ETA pressure gets a cadence, not a guess.

options.text: Stay quiet and let the loudest engineer drive
options.why: Abdication is not leadership — the room needs structure, and that is the EM’s job.

steps.prompt: The CEO wants a root cause in 10 minutes. You respond?

options.text: Give the most likely cause as fact
options.why: Premature certainty becomes the official story and misdirects the fix — managing up means honest uncertainty.

options.text: ‘Mitigation is underway; we’ll confirm root cause before stating it — next update in 15 minutes’
options.why: Managing up on delivery risk: acknowledge, bound the uncertainty, commit to the cadence — trust is built on reliable updates, not fast guesses.

options.text: Ignore the CEO until it’s fixed
options.why: Silence breeds escalation — proactive comms keep leadership aligned while you work.

steps.prompt: After mitigation, what makes the postmortem change behavior?

options.text: A detailed timeline only
options.why: Timelines record; action items with owners and dates change — the retrospective must produce both.

options.text: Blameless timeline, root causes, action items with owners and due dates, and a follow-up review
options.why: The module’s rule: retrospectives that change behavior have owners, dates, and a revisit — otherwise they are theater.

options.text: A private note to the engineer who shipped the bug
options.why: Individual blame teaches hiding; systemic fixes teach learning.

scenarios.title: The underperforming senior
scenarios.context: A senior engineer’s output has slipped for two quarters. The team notices. Skipping it is no longer an option — and this exact scenario appears in EM interviews.

options.text: Start a PIP immediately
options.why: A PIP without documented feedback and support is both unfair and legally fragile — process starts with clarity, not punishment.

options.text: Private, specific feedback: observed impact, expectations, support offered — documented
options.why: The people-leadership module: feedback that lands is private, behavioral, impact-linked, and paired with support — documented from the start.

options.text: Reassign their work quietly and hope
options.why: Quiet workarounds punish the team and teach the senior nothing — avoidance compounds the problem.

steps.prompt: They improve for a month, then regress. Now?

options.text: Give up — some people can’t change
options.why: One cycle is not a verdict; but the pattern now needs formal structure.

options.text: A formal performance plan: clear bar, timeline, check-ins, consequences — with HR partnership
options.why: Performance management escalates fairly: explicit expectations, support, timeline, and honest consequences — the module’s PIP discipline.

options.text: Extend informal feedback another two quarters
options.why: Endless informality is unfair to the team carrying the gap — clarity delayed is clarity denied.

scenarios.title: The AI feature launch decision
scenarios.context: Your team’s AI summarization feature passes demos but evals show 12% of summaries contain unsupported claims. Launch is scheduled Friday. You are the PM.

options.text: Launch — 88% is good enough
options.why: Unsupported claims in a summarizer are a trust defect at scale — shipping known hallucinations is a product decision with owners, and the owner would be you.

options.text: Delay the auto-publish; ship with citations, confidence display, and human review for low-confidence outputs — plus the eval gate for full launch
options.why: The GenAI PM playbook: UX for uncertainty (confidence, sources, undo), evals as the launch gate, and the discipline to not ship AI where the failure mode is unacceptable.

options.text: Cancel the feature entirely
options.why: One measured failure mode with mitigations available is not a cancellation — it is a scoped launch.

steps.prompt: How do you communicate this to executives?

options.text: ‘The AI isn’t ready’ — vague
options.why: Vagueness invites override — executives need the specific risk, the mitigation, and the business framing.

options.text: Pre-read with the eval numbers, the trust risk in business terms, the mitigated launch plan, and the full-launch gate criteria
options.why: Stakeholder communication on AI risk: numbers, business impact, plan, and the gate — the pre-read that keeps AI bets funded.

options.text: Don’t tell them; handle it quietly
options.why: Surprises destroy more trust than delays — the pre-launch review exists to put risks on the table.

blocks.body: Ambiguous mandate → **scope, milestones, dependency map, success criteria + exit conditions, risk register, stakeholder map, comms cadence**. The core artifact.
**Status that drives decisions** · dependency hygiene · unblocking as daily craft · escalation paths used deliberately · tradeoff triage under pressure · retrospectives with owners and dates.
No authority → **trust, decision logs, crisp escalations, follow-through**. Align EMs and PMs, resolve cross-team conflict, pre-read executives.
**1:1s** (the report’s meeting) · **feedback** (private, specific, impact-linked) · coaching vs managing · PIPs as fair process · psychological safety in practice.
Honest **estimation** (ranges + assumptions) · roadmap accountability · incident ownership · **managing up** on risk · saying no to protect the team.
**Hiring bar** + structured loops + debriefs · onboarding for ramp speed · ladders and calibration · retention of the irreplaceable.
Technical **vision** · debt quantified and funded · platform bets · engineering health metrics · align with product strategy.
**User → problem → why** (five whys, honestly) · market/competitive frame · **impact vs effort with assumptions stated** · critique by mechanism, not taste.
Roadmap under constraints · scoping with engineering · launch readiness · post-launch iteration loops · **saying no with a rationale**.
Success metrics **tied to user value** · funnels/cohorts/retention · A/B design + pitfalls · **debug the move before reacting** · estimation done sanely.
Story bank: leadership, conflict, failure, ambiguity — **tight STAR**, your role explicit, learning real. Questions for them prepared.
Requests/responses/latency · relational vs document DBs · **caching: speed vs staleness** · queues/async · estimate scale: users → RPS → storage → bandwidth.
REST literacy · **versioning = compatibility promises** · webhooks vs polling · developer experience is the product · rate limits, auth, deprecation policy.
SQL: joins, aggregations, windows · instrument events with taxonomies · **data-informed ≠ data-driven** · know when the data is lying.
Patterns: **chat / copilots / agents / RAG** — match to the job · evals as the launch gate · UX for uncertainty · risk with owners and mitigations · **hype filter: demos ≠ products**.
Scope → stakeholders → milestones → risks → comms plan. Show the skeleton before the detail: what, who, when, what could kill it.
Status cadence, RAID log (risks/actions/issues/decisions), escalation paths. Influence without authority = clarity + reliability.
Enough systems literacy to spot bad estimates and ask the question that unblocks: APIs, data flows, failure modes.
Stories of alignment: conflicting teams, missed dates, scope fights — resolved with process, not heroics.
Hiring bar, growth plans, feedback cadence, underperformance handling. 'Tell me about someone you grew' needs a real story.
Predictability: planning, estimation, capacity, incident ownership. The team's output is your output.
Tech debt policy, platform bets, build-vs-buy with total-cost reasoning. Strategy = sequenced choices under constraint.
Structured interviews, rubrics, calibrated panels. Your hiring bar is your culture in 2 years.
User → pain → solution → why now → why us. Structure before creativity: CIRCLES or equivalent, then insight.
North star + input metrics. 'How would you measure X?' → define, segment, guardrail. Never optimize one metric blindly.
Prioritization (RICE/impact-effort), tradeoffs, launch plans, post-launch iteration. Ship, measure, learn — on a cadence.
Systems literacy, API thinking, SQL fluency. Credibility with engineers without pretending to be one.

blocks.body: Where do errors cost little and value is high? Drafting, summarization, classification — not autonomous high-stakes decisions.
Golden sets + human calibration before launch. Quality gates in CI for prompts and models.
Show uncertainty, offer edits not autopilot, cite sources, graceful degradation. 'AI proposes, human disposes.'
Hallucination, bias, data leakage, prompt injection — name the risks, own the mitigations, instrument the failures.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a program you turned around.
answerBank.a: Structure: the red signals I found (missed milestones, unowned dependencies), how I re-scoped with explicit exit criteria, the dependency map I rebuilt across teams, the risk register with mitigations and owners, and the comms cadence that restored trust. Close with the outcome and what the turnaround taught me about early warning signs — interviewers score structured thinking and honest ownership, so I name what I got wrong first.

answerBank.q: How do you influence without authority?
answerBank.a: I build a stakeholder map, run decisions through written logs so nothing is tribal, escalate crisply with options instead of problems, and follow through relentlessly — trust compounds. When teams conflict, I reframe around the shared outcome and make the tradeoff explicit. My example: aligning two EMs and a PM on a platform migration by getting the dependency risks and the rollback plan agreed in writing before anyone committed dates.

Private, specific, documented feedback first: observed behaviors, business impact, clear expectations, and the support I’ll provide — with a check-in date. If the pattern continues, a formal plan with HR: explicit bar, timeline, and consequences. I’ve learned to start these conversations earlier than feels comfortable, because delay is unfair to the rest of the team. I can walk through a real case: what I tried, where I misread the situation, and what changed.

answerBank.q: How do you decide what to build? (product sense)
answerBank.a: I start from the user and the problem: who hurts, how often, what they do today — asking why until I hit the real need. Then I frame the market, size the opportunity, and prioritize by impact versus effort with my assumptions stated out loud so they can be challenged. I’d demonstrate with a teardown: what a product gets right, where it fails users, and what I’d change first — critiquing by mechanism, not taste.

answerBank.q: A key metric dropped 15% yesterday. Walk me through it.
answerBank.a: Before reacting, I debug: is the instrumentation intact, which segments moved, is it a real behavior change or a reporting artifact, and what shipped or happened externally in the window. I’d check funnels and cohorts to localize, look for confounders like seasonality or a partial rollout, and only then form hypotheses — ranked by likelihood — with the test that would confirm each. The discipline is: understand the move before acting on it.

answerBank.q: How do you evaluate a technical tradeoff as a PM? (build vs buy)
answerBank.a: I frame it as total cost of ownership: build cost plus maintenance, hiring, and opportunity cost versus buy cost plus integration, lock-in, and roadmap dependence. I check which parts are differentiating IP — build those — versus commodity — buy those. Then I pressure-test with engineering on reliability and scale assumptions, and I write the decision with its tradeoffs so it survives personnel changes. I’d give a real example with the numbers I used.

answerBank.q: Should we ship this AI feature? The demo is great but evals are shaky.
answerBank.a: The demo doesn’t decide — the evals do. I’d quantify the failure modes: rate, severity, and who gets hurt, then check whether UX mitigations (citations, confidence display, human review on low-confidence outputs) bound the risk acceptably for a scoped launch. If not, we delay with a clear eval gate for launch and a kill criterion. I’d bring executives a pre-read: the numbers, the business risk, the mitigated plan — because shipping known AI failures is a product decision with an owner, and I’d rather own the delay than the incident.

terminalSims.brief: Practice the leadership scenario-round command set — brief, clarify, options, decide, debrief — against a realistic canned sandbox.

commands.out:
Usage: lead <command> [options]

Commands:
  brief    Show the current scenario brief
  clarify  List the clarifying questions to ask first
  options  Lay out options with tradeoffs
  decide   Record a decision with rationale
  debrief  Review the decision afterward

SCENARIO 7 — 'The slipping quarter':
Your team is 3 weeks behind on a committed launch with 4 weeks left.
The VP asks for a plan by tomorrow. Structure: clarify, options, tradeoffs, decision.

Clarifying questions:
  1. What exactly is committed — scope, date, or both?
  2. What caused the slip — scope creep, estimation, dependency?
  3. What are the fixed constraints — headcount, dependencies, quality bar?

Options:
  A. Cut scope — ship the core, defer the rest. Tradeoff: smaller launch.
  B. Add people — Tradeoff: onboarding cost, Brooks's law risk.
  C. Move the date — Tradeoff: credibility cost, stakeholder impact.
  D. Cut quality — Tradeoff: tech debt and incident risk. (Not recommended.)

commands.cmd: lead decide --option A --rationale "Protect the date and quality; defer scope with stakeholder agreement"
commands.out:
Decision recorded: Option A.
Rationale: Protect the date and quality; defer scope with stakeholder agreement.
Rubric: clarify ✓, options ✓, tradeoffs ✓, decision ✓.

Debrief prompts:
  - What did you decide, and what did you miss?
  - What would you change with one more hour?
  - Which tradeoff was hardest to defend?

terminalSims.title: Leadership scenario CLI

terminalSims.brief: Run Fermi-style estimation drills — assumptions first, round-number math, sanity-check the answer. The reasoning chain is the grade.

commands.out:
Usage: est <command>

Commands:
  start        Begin a new estimation drill
  assumptions  State your assumptions aloud
  math         Show the round-number math
  check        Sanity-check the answer

DRILL 12: How many engineering managers does a 5,000-person tech company need?
State assumptions first. Round numbers only.

Assumptions (yours to state; example):
  - ~60% of 5,000 are in engineering ≈ 3,000
  - Span of control ≈ 7 engineers per manager
  - ~15% overhead for senior/skip-level managers

Math:
  3,000 engineers ÷ 7 per manager ≈ 430 team managers
  +15% overhead ≈ 495 → round to ~500 managers.

Sanity check:
  - 500 managers / 5,000 staff = 10% — plausible for a tech org.
  - If span were 5: ~690. If 10: ~345. Range 350–700 brackets the answer.
  Grade: chain stated, math round, sanity checked ✓

glossary.definition: Technical Program Manager: drives cross-team programs via planning, risk management, and influence without authority.
Engineering Manager: owns people, delivery, and technical direction for a team.
Risks, Actions, Issues, Decisions: the TPM's running ledger of program truth.
Driving outcomes through clarity, reliability, and stakeholder management rather than org-chart power.
The single metric capturing core product value; input metrics are its levers.
Metric that must not degrade while optimizing the primary one (e.g., fraud rate vs conversion).
PM framework: Comprehend, Identify customer, Report needs, Cut scope, List solutions, Evaluate, Summarize.
'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' — hence guardrails.
Aligning interviewers' scoring standards so hiring bars are consistent across panels.
Fixed questions + rubrics per role: the bias-reducing hiring method.
Explicit rules for when debt is taken, tracked, and repaid — strategy, not accident.

faq.q: TPM vs EM — which fits me?
faq.a: TPM: you love cross-team orchestration and process. EM: you want people ownership and delivery accountability. The course's mock circuits let you trial both interview loops before committing.

faq.q: Do I need to have managed people to interview for EM?
faq.a: Tech-lead experience (mentoring, leading projects) transfers. Be honest about scope: 'led 3 engineers on X' beats inflated titles. The behavioral module teaches scope-honest storytelling.

faq.q: How technical must a TPM/PM be?
faq.a: Systems-literate: APIs, data flows, failure modes, SQL. Enough to challenge estimates and earn engineering trust — not to write the code.

faq.q: What's the biggest PM interview mistake?
faq.a: Jumping to solutions before structuring the problem. Interviewers score the framework (user → pain → options → tradeoffs) more than the idea.

faq.q: How do I show 'AI product judgment'?
faq.a: Use-case selection (error cost vs value), eval discipline, uncertainty UX, and owned risk mitigations. The AI module's scenarios rehearse exactly this.
Same structure, higher stakes: emphasize the *system* you built (hiring bar, planning cadence, escalation path), not just the incident you heroically fixed.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to Project Management Professional (PMP) – 2026 ECO and Technical Leadership Interview Readiness (internal, not a vendor certification) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.

The math modules (Prereq Math: Logic & Proof for Technical Leadership Interview Prep, Prereq Math: Statistics & Probability for Technical Leadership Interview Prep) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 250-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 6 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.

noahTutoring.tagline: Noah is the learning driver — not a bolt-on.
noahTutoring.concept: Noah is the core learning driver of IL-18 — the panel across the table. Mentor runs your TPM/EM/PM mocks by voice and coaches your STAR stories until they are specific and honest; Philosopher probes the 'why' beneath every leadership answer; Trickster throws the curveball scenario. You walk into the real loop already battle-tested.

personas.label: Visionary
personas.style: Cuts to the fundamental truth, then projects forward. Challenges assumptions; frames everything as 'what could be.'

personas.label: Engineer
personas.style: Thinks in systems: inputs, outputs, constraints, failure modes. Concrete and actionable; quantifies; calls out trade-offs explicitly.

personas.label: Philosopher
personas.style: Asks the question beneath the question. Never rushes to answers; dwells in inquiry; repairs mental models with graduated hints.

personas.label: Mentor
personas.style: Notices effort and names it. Honest about difficulty; balances challenge with support; speaks like someone who has been where the learner is.

personas.label: Trickster
personas.style: Finds the absurd angle and the unexpected connection. Uses humor to illuminate; breaks fixation when the learner is stuck; kind, never punching down.

modulePersonaMap.why: Mentor is the voice interviewer: runs timed TPM/EM/PM mocks by voice, coaches STAR stories until they are specific and honest, debriefs with the rubric a real panel uses.
Engineer drills the technical half of leadership loops: systems literacy, API/platform reasoning, SQL-backed data literacy — structured, quantified, no bluffing.
Philosopher asks the 'why' beneath the leadership answer: what principle decides this trade-off, whose interests does this roadmap serve — the depth panels probe for.
Trickster throws the lateral scenario: the reorg mid-program, the impossible deadline, the failing vendor — practicing composure and structured thinking when the script breaks.
Visionary builds the product narrative: first-principles GenAI product thinking, roadmaps that account for model risk, the story of where the product — and the leader — are going.

voiceFirst.description: Talk with Noah via voice chat while working through modules — 5 distinct natural voices served by POST /api/noah/tts (Scholar, Narrator, Guide, Sage, Spark), plus adaptive browser speech: per-persona rate/pitch, emotion-aware delivery, lip-synced avatar. Voice-first mock interviews are the signature experience: Mentor asks, the clock runs, you answer aloud — exactly like the real loop.

adaptive.description: Review timing adapts to recall performance (docs/assets/noah-adaptive.js): quiz and drill results feed per-card intervals, so weak cards resurface sooner and mastered cards fade to maintenance. Mastery is tracked in localStorage; Noah re-sequences your next session around what is due, not what is next in the list.

courseAware.description: Noah tutors from this course's own knowledge — its answers are grounded in these modules, not generic web knowledge. If the endpoint is unreachable it degrades to a local Socratic engine with a plain notice. It never invents facts, credentials, or experience.

noahTutoring.houseRule: Bring Noah your hypothesis — not 'just give me the answer.' Attempt a card first.
howToUse: Open Noah from any module page and pick the persona mapped to that track.
Attempt the cards first — then bring Noah your hypothesis, not your blank stare.
For interview tracks: switch to voice, pick Mentor, and run the mock circuit aloud.
After every mock, ask Noah for the rubric debrief: what passed, what failed, what to drill next.
Revisit on Noah's schedule: the SM-2 scheduler will resurface what is due.

interactivityAudit.rule: Every module ships notes, flashcards, quiz, drills, a hands-on lab, and a mock task; interactivity is counted, not claimed.

studyGuide.title: Study guide: how to work IL-18 in 10 weeks
pacing: Weeks 1-3 — TPM track, modules 1-6 (~48h): program design, execution engine, cross-functional leadership, technical depth for TPMs, guided program case, TPM mock circuit.
Weeks 4-5 — EM track, modules 7-12 (~32h): people leadership, delivery ownership, hiring/growing teams, engineering strategy, guided leadership scenarios, EM mock.
Weeks 6-7 — PM track, modules 13-18 (~32h): product sense, execution, metrics/judgment, behavioral for PMs, guided product case, PM mock.

Weeks 8-9 — Technical PM + GenAI for PM, modules 19-30 (~80h): technical depth, API/platform thinking, data literacy, guided technical case, technical design reps, tech-PM mock; GenAI literacy, LLM product patterns, eval/UX for AI, GenAI playbook, risk, AI roadmapping.

Week 10 — Math + final loop, modules 31-32 + full simulation (~18h): logic & proof, statistics & probability, then a full leadership-loop simulation. Two consecutive clears on different days before the real loop.
rules: Stories are the currency — every behavioral answer gets a specific, honest STAR story.
Metrics with judgment: never quote a metric without the decision it drives.
Run every mock by voice with Mentor-Noah before the real loop.
Technical depth is non-negotiable for TPM/tech-PM loops — no bluffing.
Drills to green before the next module; re-take any quiz below 80%.
Bring Noah your hypothesis first — attempt every card before asking.
studyGuide.note: Totals are computed from module estimatedMinutes; pacing assumes ~25-30 focused hours per week.
